title: What butterfly wings have in common with barbershop poles
gist: A Nature study from the University of Exeter finds butterfly wing stripes create barbershop-pole-like 'motion dazzle' illusions during flight that mislead predatory birds about speed and direction, supported by high-speed video, simulations of ~400 European species, human touchscreen trials and genetic algorithms evolving 50,000 wing patterns.

insights.claim: Butterfly wing stripes and spots interfere with predators' motion perception, boosting false motion cues and hiding true heading, causing birds to miss during the final ballistic attack.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Insights into visual-tracking illusions have potential relevance for camouflage and computer vision research.
insights.quote: The illusions interfere with the predator’s most basic visual targeting system
insights.locator: “The stripes and spots on many butterflies’

insights.claim: The study addresses a paradox: butterflies have conspicuous patterns yet few predators can catch them mid-flight, unlike plainly colored moths that are preferred prey.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Shows conspicuousness can be a defense, not a liability.
insights.locator: The purpose of the patterns on butterfly wings

insights.claim: As butterfly wings deform while flapping, stripes shift angle and direction, producing a barbershop-pole-like illusion; the authors call this the first empirical evidence of motion dazzle from butterfly wings.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Provides a mechanism that could inform bio-inspired design.
insights.locator: In other words, the motion effects

insights.claim: Simulations of nearly 400 European butterfly species showed motion illusion patterns are widespread, and genetic algorithms evolving over 50,000 patterns selected designs strikingly similar to nature.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Suggests motion dazzle may be a major evolutionary driver.

insights.claim: Prior work found zebra stripes induce wagon-wheel and barbershop-pole illusions, and 2024 Macquarie University research showed humbug damselfish use motion dazzle.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Motion dazzle appears across multiple animal groups.

insights.claim: Troscianko predicts motion confusion is far more widespread in nature than realized, from bird wings to lizard and fish tails.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Opens a new research avenue in motion vision.
insights.quote: we think motion confusion is likely to be far more widespread in nature than previously realized
